Therefore, they gave up the idea and there was no action taken, and then this projectile was launched and that's the whole story. And this is what I learned only later, a couple of days afterwards. I say, again, I didn't have the right to question or interrogate soldiers. I was a civilian policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your report, you draw a conclusion on the origin of fire, and you base this on eye-witness statements, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Last question now, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can I let the witness answer, because he had just started answering my one-but-last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please provide the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have the last question repeated to me. Everything is going so fast and I cannot go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: My penultimate question was the following: In the conclusion, you draw on the origin of fire. Did you base this on eye-witness statements? You started by answering and by saying, "Yes, that's right," then you were interrupted. Could you please provide the rest of your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, based on the statement and information we received in the course of the day before we conducted the on-site investigation. And based on these stories and reports, we realised that this projectile was probably fired from the area that we received unconfirmed reports of and also according to the witnesses who saw the projectile flying over.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And this is my last question. These eye-witnesses saw black smoke; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes. This flying object was moving relatively slowly, let's say ten to 15 second. It produced a strange noise, and it left a black trail behind it. The altitude of flight was between 200 and 250 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva to re-examine. Sorry. Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to ask this map to be tendered into evidence, which has been annotated with a blue pen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D165, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I have a few questions for you. My first question to you relates to the information we have received during your testimony of fire and shelling from the ABiH; and if I have understood some of the evidence correctly, it is alleged that the launching of the modified air bomb from the VRS-held territory was fired in response to the fire coming from the ABiH. Now, my question is this: Can you, by pointing to the map, identify the places where the ABiH was firing from? And to be more precise, my question is: Was there any firing coming out of Hrasnica in the vicinity of the place where the modified air bomb landed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Your Honour, I never said that before that the army was involved in any activity or artillery firing against the VRS territory -- held territory. In my testimony today, I said that a scout saw something happening in the area of Bacevo, that he notified the commander of an artillery unit who then advised the 104th Brigade commander. He requested a -- a warning fire shell to be fired, but his request was not granted. There was no activity prior to that. It was a very quiet, surprisingly quiet morning. That was a rare occurrence during the war, so there were no operations carried out by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is your testimony as to the day on the 6th or 7th of April when the bomb landed. What about the previous days? Had there been any firing or shelling launched from ABiH-held territory in the previous days? And my question, of course, relates to the information we had in one of the exhibits, in which the accused alleges that he wanted to respond to the days of fire that had come out of the ABiH territory. And my question again is the same: If you can remember, are you then able to tell us where the firing and the shelling came from, from the ABiH side? Which areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: At the time there were combat operations in the area of Igman, Bijelasnica, and the Trnovo battlefield. In our area, there was a ban on the use of artillery. I cannot remember exactly whether this settlement under the control of the VRS were targeted. I cannot remember that. But I do know that in these combat operations at Igman, Bijelasnica, and Trnovo, whenever part of the territory were lost by the VRS, it was the civilians who paid the price for that in these three neighbourhood, Butmir and the others. So all the subsequent losses of territories were paid for by the civilians in terms of shelling, of these three neighbourhoods. I really cannot remember if the BH army had been active. As far as I can tell, I didn't have a chance to hear any shooting from either side. Please, I think you will understand that I was unable to cover the whole territory 24 hours a day; but in the days preceding this incident, the -- these days were quiet. And all the operations conducted in the area were in Igman, Bijelasnica, and Trnovo, exclusively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand you perfectly well, Witness. I want to be sure that I have understood you correctly in saying that in your testimony, there was no combat operation coming out of the Hrasnica area or, more precisely, coming out of the red circle you have identified on the map. Is that correct? Please answer me briefly, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My next question relates to the location of the ABiH command headquarters. You mentioned in your testimony that this -- that as far as you had heard, the command headquarters were located in a place called Kablar. Are you able to show us on the map where that was, with a pen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: It's a little bit in the bottom part of the map here. The name of the place is Kablarovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, thank you. I am being -- my attention is being drawn to the fact that you responded to my question by nodding, without saying anything. I repeat my question. Can you help us in identifying at least, if it's on the map, then by some mark; or if it is not on the map, then by indicating with an arrow in which direction Kablar was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is excellent. Thank you, Witness. And my last question relates to your instructions to the UNMOs who came to the site of explosion. You have told us that you secured the area, but I wish to know if you gave any particular instructions to the UNMOs regarding their attempt to conduct their own investigation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes. When I informed the judge from the police station as well as the CSB in the city about what had happened, I sought support from a team in Sarajevo because it was an incident of larger proportions. I personally went to see the UNMOs, and I told them that as soon as conditions were in place, a team will visit the scene. And I also warned them or drew their attention to the fact that it would be better for them to remain in their headquarters for a while because people were in panic and aggravated, because there a lot of casualties and lot of shelling that all the neighbourhoods had been exposed to. I asked them to keep a low precisely because people lost patience with you and everything else. So many bad things had been happening, so I asked them to stay put for a while; and as soon as tensions simmered down, I said I would personally come to fetch them and take them to the scene, which I did. Quite simply I was afraid that something would happen that would get out the control with the people -- with a local people, and this is what I told them, in essence. I think they took my advice seriously and they realised I was right because the reaction of the local community was terrible, and I really wanted to prevent anything uncontrollable from taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you order them to be locked up in a building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: No. All I know is that two policemen secured this building, but they were not locked up. They just secured the building to prevent any possible conflicts with the local populous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you instruct the two soldiers to prevent the UNMOs from leaving the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: I simply asked them, in order to avoid any incident, I told them it would be ill-advised for them to go out before the situation became calmer because I was afraid for their safety, and all the station -- police station management agreed with me that would be the best approach. Because there was -- we imposed a general ban on any movement inside this area, civilians and everyone else, precisely for the purpose of preventing any additional incidents or additional shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But why did you not just order them to go back to their own headquarters if you did not want them to hang around the site of explosion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Not that we didn't want their presence at the place of explosion. They did visit the scene. They were worked together with us on the investigation, but we were simply afraid and we feared about their safety. Another UNPROFOR APCs arrived to the location in order to provide security for the operation of the on-site investigation, because in those days there were high tensions between the civilians and members of UNPROFOR and members of UNMO mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, you're not answering my question. My question was: Why did you not just order the UNMOs to return to their own headquarters, rather than securing them in a particular building for quite a period of time, I understand.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: They were in the building where they lived, where they resided. The observer mission resided in that building. There was no need for them to leave because we would start our investigation in an hour or two, and we didn't want to start it without them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And for how long did you order them to remain in their own house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't an order. It was an instruction, until the investigation team arrived. They were not prohibited from doing anything; but when the team arrived, it would go together, and there were also UNPROFOR observers there in vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I have a few issues I want to raise in my re-examination. Firstly, just following on from His Honour Judge Harhoff's questions about UNPROFOR, I want you to clarify and confirm to the Court that when the UNPROFOR were back in their residence, can you confirm that they were at liberty to leave, if they wanted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. After the on-site investigation, they moved wherever they liked. They went to their base towards the town. After that, they moved around freely, quite normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Were you as a member of the police and your colleagues amenable to UNPROFOR conducting an investigation into this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: I always insisted at any on-site investigation, and the military observers can confirm this. I always invited them to come, and I felt that their presence would validate my investigation. It was only when they refused for security reasons to come to an on-site investigation that they did not accompany me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, following on from the initial question His Honour Judge Harhoff asked you about ABiH activity, combat activity, I would like you to see again Prosecution Exhibit -- and I always forget the number, but I think it's 225, if that could be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And also just for the benefit of the Court, I'm going to go back to the map as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall that I showed you this document in my initial examination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, sorry, do you remember seeing it in my examination in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, in my examination, I asked you about the activity related to the VRS forces. And what I want you to do now is to look at paragraph 1 where it says the word "enemy" there. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I'm just going to read the first three lines. It says, "In the second Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade area of responsibility, at 6.00 in the morning, the enemy opened fierce fire at the Famos factory. The settlement of Grlica and Vojkovici from the area of Gradina, Igman, and Lasica." Do you see that sentence there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I want you to concentrate on the area Gradina, Igman, and Lasica. Do you know where those locations are?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes, I do. These are settlements close to the Famos factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And would you be able to mark then on the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we could have the map back on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You have the map there, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could I ask the court usher to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Which location is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: It's Lasica, under the control of the army. These were residential buildings. The civilian population lived there, and it was in the immediate vicinity of the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And who controlled that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: The BH army did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you place the letters ABiH in the middle of that circle, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you now tell the Court from that location where you have just marked to the location in the centre of Hrasnica where the incident took place, what is the approximate distance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: About a kilometre, maybe a little more, a few hundred metres more perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, sticking with the map, in cross-examination, you marked two roads leading from the tunnel. You see the two roads on the dotted blue line; one going to Hrasnica and one going on the Igman road around the mountain. Do you see them there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: On which road did vehicles travel to Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: The vehicles went to Mount Igman along the road from Glavogodna above the Stojcevac area and then on towards Igman above Kovaci and Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you mark that road with a letter V, please, the road that the vehicles took to the Igman mountain.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. Just perhaps to be clear, from the two blue dotted lines, which road are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: The one across from Igman. It was a road through the forest. We called the Road of Salvation. It was the only one that could be used by vehicles. We also called it Death Road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. And can you put the V on that road, on the dotted blue line, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, I just want to be clear. I am' not sure whether this specifically arises out of cross-examination, but the place where the witness has said that he heard the launch came from, I would just like the witness to mark that with a L, just for the purposes of clarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I will allow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you see where you marked in examination, when I asked you questions, the origin of fire point. Can you just put a L beside that point, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P545, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, counsel for the Defence, in cross-examination, asked you about whether you had included in your report the eye-witnesses that saw the launch of the projectile. Do you remember being asked those questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes. I remember being asked that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That is fine for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I ask that 65 ter 787C be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you see a document on the right-hand side in your language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what is that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: It's a criminal report against an unknown perpetrator concerning the event we have been talking about. It mentioned the time and the place. It refers to the event that happened in Hrasnica on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And just to confirm, this is the event that you yourself investigated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could now ask to move to the -- to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, Witness, the third paragraph down from the top on that page, do you see where it speaks -- do you see the name (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, this report --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... his binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: This report, Witness, does it appear to you to be an official report from the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Probably, the prosecutor's office, when it continued its investigation, came by this information and took a statement from this man who is mentioned here. But I did not do this. This must have been done by the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Nevertheless, does this appear to you to be an official and authentic report from the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask had a this document be tendered and be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, you have a submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to say that for such an important witness, an important witness to the Defence, like (redacted), I object to the tendering of this document because the witness has not been involved in the drafting of it. And the Defence would also like to ask this gentleman to be called to testify because we would have liked to cross-examine him. This gentleman gave three totally different statements, so (redacted) would be an extremely important witness for the chamber also. Perhaps the Prosecutor could call this gentleman to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And if the Prosecutor doesn't call him to testify, you will call him. Is that right what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If the Prosecutor does not wish to call him, we would like to call him, because it seems to me that he is a very important witness; he, being the source of information here, and he has provided three completely different statements. In addition, the Prosecutor could perhaps tell us why they -- he has not called him to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Sachdeva, on the question of the admissibility, the point that is being made is that this witness is not sufficiently involved or was not sufficiently involved in the preparation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, on that specific point, there have been documents that are admitted already in evidence that have not necessarily been drafted by a particular witness; and, in fact, in this examination, the witness has confirmed bomb squad reports and other reports not compiled and drafted by himself. And as a member of the police, he has validated the authenticity and confirmed that they referred to the incident that he investigated. Similarly, I would submit that is correct this applies to this particular document and that it pertains to an incident that he investigated, and he has confirmed it to be through his knowledge of it being a police officer for three or four years during the war to be an authenticity document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was prepared by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It was prepared by somebody called Enes Bezdrob. That's at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And he was the BiH prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who is Enes Bedzdrob, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Enes Bedzdrob, at that time, when this was drawn up, I don't know. But probably what I do know is that at one time he was the head of the CSB. But at the time this statement was taken, it says that he was the chief of the security centre of the CSB of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the CSB? What does that stand for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It's the Security Services Centre, Mr. President, or Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, could we please go to the top of this document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Absolutely. If the page could be -- if the first page could be brought back and on the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, could you please explain to us what this document really is. It looks to me as if it's an indictment, but I'm not having doubts about what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, from my limited knowledge of the system in the former Yugoslavia, this would be charges that are being brought up by the police, which are then sent to the public prosecutor, and typically the charges include the details of the case, a brief description, and other important facts in evidence that -- that would be given to the public prosecutor to decide whether an official indictment should be brought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber rules that the document can't be tendered through this witness. It is, of course, open to the Defence to call the person mentioned in it what's his name? If you scroll down we can see the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Might I make a brief -- in the interests of transparency, might I make a brief submission in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, before I continue, can I just ask that the previous document be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Remind me which one was that? What was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That was the document that we had submissions on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be admitted as P546.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I won't be much longer. I'm going take you back to cross-examination, and do you recall, firstly, counsel for the Defence asking you questions about whether there were reporters at the scene on the day of the incident? Do you recall those questions or that question?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please answer again. The interpreter could not hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I remember being asked about the presence of reporters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, indeed, your answer was, "There were reporter. There was a big crowd as far as I was able to state -- as far as I was able to notice." You said, "It was clearly seen that something major had happened in Hrasnica, and I did notice a few reporter vehicles." Can you elaborate a little bit of what you saw and what you now with respect to the journalists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were two UNPROFOR APCs and a couple of jeeps, and I noticed people with cameras near the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Were you able to ascertain whether the people with cameras were -- were from Bosnia-Herzegovina or were they foreign journalists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: I think that those were foreign journalists. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to play a video and that is an excerpt from a video. That is the excerpt that Your Honours have granted the Prosecution to add on its witness -- exhibit list, and the video ERN is V000-7160.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before you allow or not the Prosecution's request, if we see this video, if you allow for this video, will I be allowed to ask a few questions to the witness? I did not ask these questions because the video had not been shown so far. So this is my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, you must tell us about the video and explain how the contents of the video arise from cross-examination. Is this the video that you had mentioned at the beginning of the session?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It is the excerpt from -- from a BBC video that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I had the impression that you would have sought to have it played during examination-in-chief. In any event, please explain what it is and how it arises from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I submit that it does arise out the cross-examination because counsel had asked the witness about journalists on the scene. And I have asked the witness from his knowledge whether these journalists were foreign or journalists from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and his response was that he thought they were foreign. This video, in the Prosecution's submission, purports to show the aftermath of the incident that is the subject of this witness' examination, and it is from the BBC; namely, a foreign news company. And therefore, in my submission, it does arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say it arises because the witness was cross-examined about journalists being on the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, although my colleague, Ms. Isailovic is questioning this witness, you may remember that at the beginning we, as the Defence, had no objection to this being shown, and we expected to see that during examination-in-chief. Therefore, I see no reason why one can say that this is necessary to do this at this point in time. Why wasn't that done during the examination-in-chief; and in that respect, we believe that it is up to you to assess this motion and to decide thereupon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Tapuskovic, the proper basis for opposing is not that it wasn't done in chief but that it doesn't arise out of cross-examination. What do you have to say to that, or Ms. Isailovic? Does it arise properly out of cross-examination. That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, Your Honour, it does not arise from the cross-examination, which is why before your decision, I said that if you came up with a positive decision we need additional questions after we see this video, because it's almost as if Mr. Sachdeva was going through a new in-chief with this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are of the view that you have not really explained what the video shows. What are the contents of the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm quite able to do that. I don't know whether if indeed you allow plea to show it whether--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. Not to show it, to tell us. We want to know what it purports to show.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well t purports to show it is a 20 or 30 news bulletin about an incident in Hrasnica, and it then pans to -- to what the Prosecution submits was the location of the incident that we've just been hearing evidence on. So it is essentially a video of the aftermath of the 7th of April 1995 in Hrasnica, at least that is what the Prosecution submits, and that is why I wanted to show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So essentially it doesn't have anything to do with journalists?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber rules that it does not arise out the cross-examination, and we will not allow the video to be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I just have one request? I understand your order and that I'm bound by that. In truth, you know, because of the time constraints I had, it was my oversight. Of course, I intended to show it in my examination-in-chief; however, because of time constraints I forgot. And upon questions about Defence counsel, and in particular the questions related to the journalists, I, in my submission, thought that it did arise out of cross-examination. I understand Your Honour's ruling on that, but what I would ask that is the next witness, who also will speak to this incident in brief, whether I could show the video to the next witness in my examination-in-chief. I ask permission because it's not on the list provided to the Defence beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will allow that. If you can lead it through the next witness, I don't see why not. There's the very technical objection that it's not on the list, but I don't think the Defence will insist on that and I will not insist on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, okay. My final question: Witness 57, at the very beginning of cross-examination - and I'm seeking a clarification here - counsel for the Defence showed you the aerial photograph with the houses at the location of the incident. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the precise question by counsel, and that's on page 25, line 21 is: "Witness, you said that there were a lot of material damage caused by the war and particularly there in Hrasnica. I presume that at the time this incident occurred on the 7th April, there weren't very many houses in which you could live in at the time. Is that right, in Hrasnica." And your response was: "What do you mean by uninhabitable houses." And the next question was: "Again, you mention there was material damage caused by the war. This incident occurred on the 7th of April 1995; therefore, a long while after the beginning of the war -- after the beginning of convict. So my question to you is this: At this particular point in time, did the damage caused by military operations render these houses uninhabitable." And your answer was: "Yes. There were such houses, but most of the houses were unsafe to live in and, mostly, they were in the vicinity of the confrontation lines; whereas, the other houses in Hrasnica, Butmir and other settlements that were damages as a result of the war were places where did live, because they had no other places to live". I just don't want there to be any confusion with respect to the particular houses that counsel was speaking about. And so the houses that were in the vicinity of the location where the bomb exploded, were these houses -- were people living in those houses at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-57
utterances.text: Yes. People lived in those houses at the time. And the proof is that people were living in the house where the bomb exploded as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness 57, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The next witness is W-116.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much time is allocated for the examination-in-chief for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: One hour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 92 ter, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: One and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: An hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just to inform you that you had requested the Prosecution requested protective measures on your behalf, and the Court has granted the measures in the face -- in the name of face distortion and pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm now going to hand you a piece of paper with your personal details, and I want you to confirm to the Court that those details are correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, these are my personal details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I ask that be admitted under seal, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes P547, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 116, do you remember giving statements to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 14th of November, 1995; the 26th of February, 1996; the 11th of March, 1997; and the 28th of November, 1997.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Were you given an opportunity to review and read over those statements in the -- yesterday in my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes. I was given an opportunity to read and review the statements that I made earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Upon review of those, statements can you now confirm to the Court that the contents are accurate and true, to the best of your recollection and knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I can confirm that all my statements are true and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Could I can ask that 65 ter 03108 be brought up and for it not to be broadcast, please. I think there is a slight technical hitch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you're more fortunate than we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, these things sometimes happen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can we have the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: All right. Witness, on the left-hand side, you'll see a statement from the 14th of November, 1995. I just want you to look at the bottom and confirm that that is indeed your signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If it can be scrolled down to the bottom, please. No, of the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I were to ask you questions today in court, would the answers that you give to the Court reflect the contents of this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P548, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can I now have 65 ter 03109 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, again, same procedure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: This is a statement from the 26th of February, 1996. Do you see your signature, and do you confirm that that is indeed your signature.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, again, if I was to ask you questions in court, would your answers reflect the contents of this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I ask that this statement be admitted under seal, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P549, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The next 65 ter is 03110, if that could be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the statement there from the 11th of March, 1997, and can you confirm your signature on the bottom right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: At the bottom on the right-hand side of the left-hand side document, which is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Again, if I was to ask you questions in court, would your answers reflect the content of this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this be admitted under seal, and I note that the part of the statement that deals with an incident on the 29th of June, 1995 at boulevard, Mese Selimovica Street, is an incident that has been dropped and removed pursuant to the 73 bis order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes P550.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Lastly, if I could have 65 ter 03111 brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 116, same questions: Is that your statement from the 28th of November, 1997, and is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes, but this was the 28th of November, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: The date of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. I thought I said 28th of November, but thank you for that. If I was to ask you questions again in court, would your reflect the content of this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I ask that this statement be admitted under seal, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P551, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 116, during the war were you a police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What was your exact title?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: I was a forensic technician in the public security centre in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Were you assigned to a particular police station; and if so, which one was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: I was in the centre for public security of Sarajevo, so we covered all the police stations on the territory of the city of Sarajevo, including Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And as a forensic technician what was - and very briefly - your duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: As a forensic technician, my duties were to go with a team and the team leader, usually a crime inspector; and in serious cases, there always had to be a judge and court experts. Together we would go to the scene of the crime and collect all the relevant information, which would later be used to reconstruct the crime. My task was, first, when we arrived on site, we would get information from the uniformed policemen on the site whose task had been to secure the scene number your arrival. They would collect the basic information about what had happened and then they would brief us. After that, the team leader, who was usually a judge or a criminal inspector, would decide how the inspection or the investigation would proceed. My task would be to photograph the scene of the crime; to photograph the broader view, the general view, showing all the roads leading up to the scene, the surrounding buildings, and so on; and then to take photographs of the site itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: After that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also prepare sketches of the scene?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes. My next task would be to make sketches of the scene indicating the most important details relevant for the crime. And the sketch would then be appended to the photographic documentation. That would be two parts of one whole, and then the third part would be the forensic report. So those would be the three different parts of my contribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you speak about going to the scene of the crime, what types of crimes are you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: As a forensic technician, I worked on all kinds of crimes, commonly crimes occurring in peacetime, such as burglaries, murders, serious traffic accidents; but also in wartime, war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Ant I want just to concentrate on the war and, in particular, the time-period of August 1994 through November 1995. What types of incidents did you investigate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: In this period, because Sarajevo was being shelled intensively, most of these on-site investigations had to do with shelling or sniping on Sarajevo and its citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sticking to the shelling, did you investigate an incident in Hrasnica on the 7th of April, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did you go to the scene?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes, I did, with the entire team. With me was a ballistics expert and there were inspectors from the crime investigation department from Hrasnica and also UN observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you. When you went to the scene and when you did your investigation, did you produce a sketch of the incident site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could ask that 65 ter 00107 be brought up and, again, for it not to be broadcast, please. If the right-hand side of the B/C/S version, if the next page could be shown, please. And for the benefit of the Court, the translation, the English translation is 00620089. So by my counting, that's page 10 of the English version. It starts on page 10 of the English version. Page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, on the right-hand side, do you see the sketch, your sketch that you made at the scene?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes, but I see only the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is that your sketch, or rather, is that the legend from your sketch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes. That is the legend pertaining to the sketch and the description of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if we can could go to the next page, please, I'm not sure whether this page and the next page can be shown together as the full sketch?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is that your sketch, Witness 116?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is my sketch. The sketch of the scene of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And on this sketch, can you -- can you say where the bomb exploded? Is that marked there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's indicated here where there is a group of traces. It fell on the house marked 14. In the legend, it's the house under number 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. The 14, that is on the corner of the right-hand side by the square; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you see a dotted line on the top left-hand corner of the square?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-116
utterances.text: It represents the direction from which the projectile arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this sketch be admitted into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We are at the time for the break. We will adjourn and resume tomorrow at 9.00. What is the number for this?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be P552, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We're adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 18th day of April, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
